# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

</document>
response:
Sections 1–5 are a strong re-analysis. They put numbers on several problems with the Halden paper that could previously only be argued in principle, and the microdata findings on attrition and on manager-reported versus record-based output are important. Sections 6–8 and the headline conclusion go well beyond that evidence. The comment's own data, and the Varden trial it cites, contradict the claim that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact."

The arithmetic in Table 2 checks out (95.1/0.8 = +18.9%; 98.4/0.859 = +14.6%; 95.4/0.861 = +10.8%), as do the hours ratios and the real-revenue figure (1.014/1.041 ≈ −2.6%). One number does not.

## Where the comment is strong

- **Attrition (§1).** If the microdata show seven of the nine withdrawals happening after the schedule began, and six citing workload or output, then the working paper's description ("during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons") is wrong on both counts. That is a significant finding, and the Halden authors should respond to it.
- **Manager index vs. records (§2).** 19 of 23 organisations went in the same direction (sign test p ≈ 0.001), so the gap is systematic and not noise. The comment explains it without alleging bad faith, which is the right tone.
- **Actual hours (§3).** Measuring hours with time-tracking software confirms what Halden only conceded in its Limitations section.
- **Sectors (§5).** The point that the per-hour metric guarantees a "gain" in every sector is correct. The three retail organisations with records (−11.2%) are a small sample but point the same way as Varden's counter offices.

## Problems in sections 1–5

**1. The abstract overstates what was corrected.** It says "Correcting the first three [problems], the gain … falls … to 10.8%." The first problem is attrition, and Table 2 never corrects for it: the four rows adjust only the output measure and the hours denominator. Attrition is documented but not quantified. A bounding exercise would fix this, for example assigning the nine withdrawers output indices from 80 to 95 and showing the range of the pooled estimate. As written, the abstract misdescribes Table 2.

**2. Table 2 changes the sample at every row.** The rows cover 61, 23, 27 and 17 organisations, so each step mixes a measurement correction with a change of sample. The clean comparison runs all four specifications on the same 17 organisations, starting with the as-reported figure for those 17. Without that, the reader can't tell how much of the fall from 23.4% to 10.8% is the correction and how much is the subset. The Data note admits the subsets aren't random, but the Conclusion then generalises the subset figures to the whole pilot ("overstated output by roughly four points"; "overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points").

**3. The hours breakdown doesn't add up.** The comment attributes the extra time to +0.7 hours per day on four days (2.8 hours) plus 1.6 hours logged on the day off, which is 4.4 hours above 32. That implies about 36.4 actual hours, but the reported figure is 34.6, only 2.6 hours above 32. Different subsamples or a different reference point for the "+0.7" might explain it, but as presented the two figures are inconsistent and need reconciling.

**4. Records may not capture all output.** Billable hours, tickets closed and units produced are narrower than whatever the manager was rating, and some of them, billable hours especially, are partly inputs. The 19-of-23 pattern still points to optimistic rating. But "overstates output relative to organisations' own records" is more defensible than treating the records as true output, and some of the 3.8-point gap could reflect what the records leave out.

**5. CPI is a rough deflator here.** Organisation revenue is better deflated with sector producer prices, or compared against revenue growth at similar organisations that weren't in the pilot. Revenue is also not a meaningful output measure for the non-profit participants. None of this rescues the Halden revenue claim, which remains weak.

## Where the comment overreaches

**6. "Entirely an artifact" contradicts the comment's own results.** After every correction it makes, the comment still finds a 10.8% gain per actual hour. It then attributes that remainder to novelty without testing the idea (point 7). It also leaves out the strongest evidence against its conclusion. In Varden's case-processing offices:

- treatment was randomised, which addresses selection;
- output came from administrative records and hours from timesheets, which addresses measurement;
- there was a contemporaneous control group;
- the result was +12.5% output per actual hour (CI +6.9 to +18.4) at nine months.

That design rules out selection and measurement as explanations. Only novelty remains as a possible artifact, and it is unproven. The comment calls Varden's counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature" but never mentions the case-processing result produced by the same design in the same trial. That is selective use of evidence. The Varden counter offices also showed +6.7% per actual hour.

**7. The novelty argument is untested, and the test was available.**

- It draws a straight line through two survey points (0.61 SD at month three, 0.29 at month six) to predict a return to baseline at about month ten. Two points can't tell a linear decline from one that levels off.
- Self-reported energy is not output per hour. The argument assumes the residual gain is driven by energy without showing it.
- The comment has the pilot's **monthly** output index. If novelty is the explanation, output per hour should fall over months one to six. The obvious check was not run, or not reported.
- "The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" is a fair point about durability. But "entirely an artifact" is also a positive claim, and the comment's own phrase "six months is not long enough to distinguish" applies to it too. The supportable conclusion is that durability is unknown.

**8. Section 7 misdescribes the Varden meetings analysis.**

- "Selected for analysis after the results were known": Varden says the calendar data were collected at month six, at managers' request, before the nine-month results.
- "Fitted to a subgroup": the seven offices are the entire treated case-processing stratum, not a subset chosen from it.
- "Should not be cited as a mechanism": Varden didn't present it as one. Its authors said the analysis was unregistered, rests on seven offices, "cannot establish a mechanism," and registered a confirmatory test.

The comment misses the strongest objection, which is that meeting time was measured only in month six, with no pre-period. The 3.3-hour gap may therefore be a difference in levels that existed before the trial, not a change caused by it.

There's also a tension. If removing low-value meetings explains part of the gain, then that part is a real efficiency gain and not an artifact. Dismissing the meetings hypothesis is what makes "entirely an artifact" sustainable, so the comment has a stake in that dismissal it should acknowledge.

**9. The conclusion is stated more strongly than the body supports.** "In our assessment" doesn't soften "entirely." The evidence in sections 1–5 supports this:

> The Halden pilot overstated the per-hour gain by more than half. Attrition, which we could not correct, likely overstates it further. Where output depends on staff presence, reduced hours reduce output per employee. Whether a remaining per-hour gain of roughly 10–12% in non-coverage work persists is unresolved; the one randomised trial finds it at nine months, and its durability is untested.

That is still a strong correction to the Halden paper, and it doesn't claim more than the data show.

## Recommendations to the authors

- Run all Table 2 specifications on a common sample of 17 organisations, and add a bound for attrition.
- Reconcile the hours breakdown with the 34.6-hour total.
- Use the monthly output index to test for decline across months one to six.
- Address the Varden case-processing result directly.
- Revise §7 to describe the Varden analysis accurately. The missing pre-period is the stronger criticism anyway.
- Bring the Abstract and Conclusion in line with the Data note.

The closing recommendations (record-based output, actual hours, comparison groups, 18+ month follow-up, analysis of all enrolled organisations) are exactly right. They are also what the comment's own evidence calls for, which supports concluding that the question remains open rather than settled in the negative.
